commenti.body:
If you don't have any base knowledge of film and film analysis, I'd argue the best start is a first-year film studies textbook. 

The best one out there IMO is Bordwell and Thompson's "Film Art: an Introduction". It's been going for decades and is updated every year, so you can get one for like 2022 or whatever for really cheap. I also think you can go to their website and actually download the book for free.

Totally worth having. You can read it straight through or just go straight to an interesting chapter, but I think it's fully worth starting from the start to get a real sense of film history.

Second u/snarpy’s recommendation of Film Art. 

Also recommend Story by Robert McKee. I write fiction (two published novels) and was, for a time, head fiction editor of a literary journal. McKee’s book is the best I’ve read when it comes to narrative construction. 

[This is another free resource about visual and narrative techniques used in movies.](https://filmcolossus.com/how-to-watch-a-movie/) What they how, how to identify them. 

Also recommend any film book by Robert Kolker.

I've been doing research for a pet project about horror movie history, here's what I've come across so far and would recommend:

"From Caligari to Hitler: A Psychological History of the German Film", Kracauer, S. (1947). 

Not a book, but [this](https://offscreen.com/view/kabuki_kurosawa_part_2) article titled "The Effects of Kabuki on Akira Kurosawa’s Auteurism" was interesting. Similarly: [This](https://www.jstor.org/stable/3661109) article, also about Japanese cinema. Pivoting to the "blaxploitation" subgenre, [this](https://www.studiobinder.com/blog/what-is-blaxploitation-definition/) article.

Lastly: [This](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g5WbeoP_B8E) video! Focuses a bit more on film theory/technique than film analysis, covers the "soviet montage" subgenre and the ideas behind it. Very interesting.
Appreciate it!! That sounds perfect bc I don't know any base knowledge apart.

Love the Mckee rec, I feel like narrative construction is a perfect way to frame what I am hoping to get better at. Is the link below the one you are referencing? Just want to double check because it says for screen-writing, but I know you right fiction novels. Would be cool if it applies to all type of writing! Thanks so much. 

https://www.amazon.com/Story-Structure-Substance-Principles-Screenwriting-ebook/dp/B0042FZVOY
Thank you so much, especially for providing all the hyperlinks. The video seems great!
That’s the one! It applies to all types of writing!
